title: Trump Announces Ban on Canadian Alcohol Imports, Escalating Trade Conflict
summary:
On Tuesday, president Donald Trump announced a plan to ban import of a range of Canadian products, escalating the already tense tariff disputes between the U.S. and its neighbor to the north. The restrictions — which are set to go into effect on Sept. 29 — will encompass alcoholic beverages including wine, spirits, malt beer as well as dairy products and motor parts. The latest in the ongoing tariff tug-of-war, this proclamation came amid a growing trade conflict between the two countries.

content:
On Tuesday, president Donald Trump announced a plan to ban import of a range of Canadian products, escalating the already tense tariff disputes between the U.S. and its neighbor to the north. The restrictions — which are set to go into effect on Sept. 29 — will encompass alcoholic beverages including wine, spirits, malt beer as well as dairy products and motor parts.

The latest in the ongoing tariff tug-of-war, this proclamation came amid a growing trade conflict between the two countries. In July, Trump threatened to add a 50 percent levy on Canadian products including alcohol, milk, and auto parts, set to go into effect on Aug. 19. After glimpses of a potential negotiation, the U.S. and Canada failed to reach an agreement, and the tariffs took effect on Aug. 22. In response, Canada announced retaliatory levies on $20 billion of U.S. goods, which began on Tuesday and spurred Trump’s announcement of the forthcoming ban.

The Trump administration’s strong-arming began in April 2024 with the announcement of the Liberation Day tariffs, to which Canada responded with a province-wide ban, stripping U.S. alcohol products from retail and bar shelves across the country. Canada’s booze ban contributed to considerable dings to the export revenue from the U.S. wine, beer, and spirits industries in 2025.

Whether there is room for trade negotiations remains to be seen. Officials from both countries — reliable trading partners — remained steadfast in their hopes for a potential deal, though no efforts have been made to advance negotiations yet.

title: 9 of the Best White Wines from Italy’s Campania
summary:

content:
Campania, the southern Italian region on the Tyrrhenian Sea, is perhaps best known for Aglianico, the marvelous red variety that is sometimes referred to as “the Barolo of the South.” If you haven’t tried Aglianico, here are some recommendations from my column earlier this year.

Beyond Aglianico, Campania, with its volcanic soils deposited by Mount Vesuvius, offers several notable but lesser-known white varieties that produce some of the more exciting wines on the southern Italian landscape.

With many wine lovers gravitating toward lighter, lower-alcohol whites, Campania’s offerings are an obvious choice and deserve more consideration. They are mostly unoaked and aged in stainless steel tanks.

Along with Campania’s soils, its hilly terrain provides a cooling influence that preserves acidity in the grapes. This translates to fresh and flavorful wines that pair well with fish, shellfish, cheeses, all manner of vegetables, and other lighter foods.

Among them is Fiano, the grape of the celebrated Fiano di Avellino denomination, named after the city and province of Avellino. With its crisp acidity, Fiano is marked by its freshness but also its vivid fruit, floral, and herbal notes. While relatively light, it can be complex and multi-layered.

Other notable white varieties from Campania include Greco and Falanghina. As the name suggests, Greco is thought to have originated in Greece, and in the top Greco di Tufo denomination, Tufo refers to tuffa, the chalky, compressed volcanic soil that gives the wine its minerality. Falanghina, which may have also come from Greece, may be slightly less complex but produces refreshing wines for everyday drinking. There’s also an example of the ancient Coda di Volpe variety on the list below.

Many of Campania’s most prominent wine regions are near Mount Vesuvius, an active volcano, and Mount Taburno. Beyond Avellino and the noted Irpinia region, other important areas include the province of Benevento and its Sannio subregion.

The white wines of Campania sometimes remind me of Etna Biancos, the high-acid, mineral-driven wines from the Mount Etna region of Sicily. Although the grapes are different, the style is similar: refreshing, textured volcanic wines that represent some of the better white-wine values.

Here are nine of the best white wines from Campania.

Tenuta Scuotto Fiano di Avellino 2023

There’s a nice richness to this Fiano, with aromas and flavors of peach, honey, and herbs, most notably a touch of mint. There’s also an almond hint and a mineral backdrop. Starting with the 2026 vintage, the property is certified organic. While many people think these wines should be drunk within a year or two of bottling, this one suggests that they can develop a richer character as they age.

Price: $20
Buy This Wine

Villa Matilde Greco di Tufo di Altavilla 2024

This crisp, lemony wine has good complexity with a green apple note joining the citrus. An herbal touch offsets the fruit and the wine is marked by a long, mineral finish. Easy to drink, refreshing, and memorable.

Price: $23
Buy This Wine

Cantine Iorio Falanghina Beneventano 2025

Cantine Iorio only produces Aglianico and Falanghina, and this Falanghina from the province of Benevento is grown in limestone and clay soil. Light straw in color, its rich fruit evokes honeydew melon with touches of honeysuckle, white flowers, almond, white pepper, and menthol. Aged for four months in stainless steel tanks, it’s a “summer” wine you’ll enjoy all year.

Price: $18
Buy This Wine

Cautiero ‘Trois’ Greco 2023

Cautiero, a winery located near Mount Taberno, farms organically and uses four or five days of skin contact for its white wines. This golden-colored orange wine is bursting with concentrated fruit flavors, including candied apple, peach, apricot, lemon, and hints of grapefruit and honey. The flavors are supported by a mild tannic grip and excellent acidity.

Price: $18
Buy This Wine

Contrada Fiano di Avellino 2024

This fresh, delicately savory wine has a nice richness that frames aromas and flavors of lemon-lime and a touch of honey. Hints of tomato leaf, herbs, and saline provide interesting accents along with the long, mineral finish. The ’23 is being sold here.

Price: $23
Buy This Wine

Fattoria La Rivolta Fiano Taburno Sannio

Luscious fruit is punctuated by pronounced minerality in this notable Fiano. There’s a nice round quality to the wine, which shows apple, strawberry, and orange notes with hints of thyme and white flowers. La Rivolta has used organic farming practices for almost three decades.

Price: $25
Buy This Wine

Fattoria La Rivolta Coda di Volpe Taburno Sannio 2024

Fattoria La Rivolta also makes a notable expression of Coda di Volpe — a lesser-known white variety in Campania — showcasing its fresh and elegant profile. Flint and almond hints punctuate aromas and flavors of white peach, apricot, and a touch of vanilla. The wine has a nice roundness and a long, mineral finish.

Price: $21
Buy This Wine

Iovine Falanghina 2024

This is an excellent, under-$20 Falanghina marked by its freshness, ripe fruit, and a slight spritz when first poured. Aromas and flavors of citrus, mainly orange, are joined by pineapple and herbal notes that lead to a long, mineral finish.

Price: $18
Buy This Wine

Villa Matilde Fiano di Avellino ‘Montelapio’ 2024

This is an enjoyable, easy-drinking wine that could easily be your house white for casual sipping or pairing with simple fish and chicken dishes. It offers green and red apple notes, a hint of citrus, and the region’s signature minerality. Crisp and refreshing.

Price: $23
Buy This Wine

Next up: Affordable Barolos to drink now

title: 7 NFL Teams Whose Fans Have Iconic Game Day Drink Orders — From the Chicago Handshake to the Kansas City Ice Water
summary:
Every September, NFL fans gather together to christen a new football season. This ritual of renewal carries a feeling of fresh promise and boundless hope, since no team has been officially eliminated from playoff contention yet. It also provides a convenient means to gather together with good friends and drink something. What exactly gets consumed can depend on the team. While beer is the universal choice of tailgaters everywhere and likely will remain as such despite the beer industry’s well-documented struggles, certain fandoms may reach for a singular beverage when it’s time to switch things up a bit.

content:
Every September, NFL fans gather together to christen a new football season. This ritual of renewal carries a feeling of fresh promise and boundless hope, since no team has been officially eliminated from playoff contention yet. It also provides a convenient means to gather together with good friends and drink something.

What exactly gets consumed can depend on the team. While beer is the universal choice of tailgaters everywhere and likely will remain as such despite the beer industry’s well-documented struggles, certain fandoms may reach for a singular beverage when it’s time to switch things up a bit. More often than not, these are hyper-specific beverages that share a unique connection with the city or region the team represents. This makes them more than beverages. They’re more like liquid points of civic pride.

The connections forged between these drinks and a team’s fan base carries DNA that’s not unlike a dive bar. They aren’t created. They’re earned. Some franchises boast “official” team cocktails that are sold during game day, but these tend to be conjured up in conjunction with a spirit brand. They may be tasty, but they don’t have the character that can only be developed outside the stadium.

These are the drinks we’re exploring here. They aren’t necessarily beloved for their deliciousness. While flavor is king in most situations, when it comes to the NFL drinking experience, sometimes tradition usurps taste. And yes, we are well aware any article exploring what NFL fans drink on game day can be a tidy list of all 32 teams with the word “beer” next to them, but what’s the fun in that? With that in mind, here are seven NFL teams with the most devout game day drinking traditions.

Team: Baltimore Ravens
Drink: Orange Crush

This may initially confuse fans of the Denver Broncos fans, some of whom may be old enough to remember the team’s vaunted Orange Crush defense in the late ’70s. In Baltimore, however, the Orange Crush references a regional cocktail that’s easy to drink and kind of a pain in the butt to make — at least, a pain in the upper arm. The drink requires the person making it to squeeze the hell out of two oranges and collect as much juice as they possibly can, which could get a little tedious for people prepping the drink for a large Ravens watch party. But combining the juice with vodka, triple sec, and lemon-lime soda in a highball loaded with crushed ice can make the effort feel worthwhile after the first sip. The prep work that goes into the drink may be why the locals take it seriously. So seriously, in fact, the state of Maryland made it the official state cocktail in 2025.

Team: Chicago Bears
Drink: Chicago Handshake (A shot of Malört and Old Style Beer)

Of course Chicago and Malört are in the same sentence for this exercise. Chicagoans are a hardy bunch that rally around the infamously bitter liqueur almost like it’s some sort of liquid deity. Pairing a shot of the acquired taste with a can of Old Style Beer is practically a citywide sacrament even when there’s not a Bears game going on. Drinking the one-two punch on game day seems like the holiest of times to engage in this ritual. This can look strange to an outsider, given Malört’s sordid reputation for tasting like the night your first girlfriend dumped you. But that may be the point. It may be a weird practice, but it’s a Chicago practice. That’s what ultimately matters, just as long as nobody mentions that Old Style actually comes from Wisconsin.

Team: Dallas Cowboys
Drink: Frozen Margarita

The Frozen Margarita is a serious point of pride for Dallas drinkers, and rightly so. “Big D” gave birth to the frigid concoction in 1971, and the city’s tourism board celebrates this through the promotion of its Margarita Mile self-guided tour. Cowboys owner Jerry Jones and his administrative minions seem to understand the drink and its city-based lore. The team brings the party into the stadium on game day by selling fans the Cowboyrita — essentially a ginormous Frozen Marg made with Hornitos (either Plata or Reposado). This technically makes the Frozen Margarita an “official” team cocktail equipped with a silly name and a fancy brand partnership. But the refreshing cocktail is just as easy to make at home for loyal Dallas-area fans as they watch their team do Dallas Cowboy things, which these days includes failing to live up to their hype.

Team: Green Bay Packers
Drink: Wisconsin Old Fashioned

Yes, Packer-backers drink copious amounts of beer on Sundays. It’s part of the deal being in a state that’s just as famous for its alcohol consumption as it is its cheese. But when they want something a little fancier on game day, there’s no better choice than to imbibe in a drink that frankly feels like it can only come from a place like Wisconsin. This is definitely not the Old Fashioned found outside the Badger State. Rather than the classic bourbon-based build, this version traditionally stars brandy, sugar cubes, a muddled cherry and orange wedge, and either seltzer or lemon-lime soda alongside the expected Angostura bitters. It’s not a riff on a classic. It’s its own entity, and Packer fans and Wisconsinites in general are fiercely loyal to the beverage. If you’re in town for a game and request an Old Fashioned, understand there is a very high likelihood that this is the drink you’re going to get.

Team: Kansas City Chiefs
Drinks: Horsefeather and Kansas City Ice Water

Chiefs fans have been spoiled by their team’s success over the last several years, 2025’s forgettable campaign notwithstanding. That pampered vibe spills over into the world of game day cocktails, as fans tend to gravitate toward a couple regional favorites, the Horsefeather and the Kansas City Ice Water. The Horsefeather is most often historically linked to KC and is basically a Moscow Mule riff where rye whiskey replaces the vodka base and served in a highball instead of a kleptomania-inducing copper mug. The Kansas City Ice Water is also a highball, one built around a split base of gin and vodka, triple sec, and lime juice topped with lemon-lime soda. While both are easy-drinking, the Kansas City Ice Water refreshes while the Horsefeather delivers a spicy kick. As such, it theoretically may behoove indecisive Chiefs fans to indulge in the former the first half of the season before switching to the latter at around Week 9 when the temperature starts to drop.

Team: Minnesota Vikings
Drink: Grape Ape

The Vikings and the Bears have little in common outside of being in the same division. But like their NFC North rivals in Chicago, the game day drink of choice for Minnesota fans involves a regional shot that only a local can truly love. The Grape Ape was invented at The Loon Cafe in downtown Minneapolis in 1995, in the middle of a decade where flavored vodka was booming and most shots were arguably created as a dare. This may explain the shot’s original unorthodox build of Absolut Citron, sweet and sour mix, the locally-produced Buddy’s Grape Soda, and a touch of Sprite. Plenty of variations have emerged in the past three decades, from using straight vodka to dropping Chambord into the recipe to supposedly improve its taste. Even with these tweaks, the shot remains sweet, fruity, and most crucial of all, purple like the Vikings’ home jerseys.

Team: Philadelphia Eagles
Drink: Fish House Punch

 

Philly sports fans are a wily bunch. They once booed and threw snowballs at Santa Claus. Their old football stadium housed a jail for fans. They started ripping a baseball stadium apart during its final game. So it makes perfect sense that their game day drink of choice is the legendary Fish House Punch, a drink so potent, it allegedly made George Washington lose his mojo for three days. Granted, he allegedly knocked back 13 of them in one session. Still, the drink should arguably come with a warning for any Eagles fans seeking out a pre-game tipple. The punch delivers its wallop in two different ways. Firstly, it’s a strong drink traditionally made with Jamaican rum, Cognac, and either peach or apple brandy. Secondly, it’s a sweeter beverage that tastes deceptively light, making it easy to forget just how much alcohol is involved. Add some local history into the mix — the drink was invented at a Philadelphia-area fishing club during colonial times — and fans have the perfect way to prepare for a Sunday full of football.

title: Does Hospitality Suffer When a Top Cocktail Bar Goes All-in on Reservations?
summary:
By 5 p.m. on most nights, a healthy line of anxious hopefuls coalesces outside the entrance of schmuck. in New York City’s East Village. content:
By 5 p.m. on most nights, a healthy line of anxious hopefuls coalesces outside the entrance of schmuck. in New York City’s East Village. For those who didn’t have the forethought to make a reservation, their only hope to procure a coveted seat is to arrive early and join the queue. When schmuck. opened in early 2025, it offered only a handful of global access reservations via Resy, which are held exclusively for American Express cardholders; now almost half the tables in the early and late seatings can be booked in advance during the week. The bar still welcomes walk-ins throughout the night, but with more tables committed to reservations, the window to squeeze in has shrunk significantly.

Reservations were once an anomaly in bars, but they’re becoming increasingly common in the upper echelon of the craft cocktail world. In the past, visiting a bar was considered an open-ended experience, one where the duration of the stay was dictated by the guest’s, not the bar’s, schedule. Patrons would patiently wait for a table and once seated, it would be theirs as long as they needed. But today, many destination bars require reservations, and the booking often comes with a built-in, and often austere, time limit.

With the prestige conferred to certain bars by international awards programs like the World’s 50 Best, some patrons have warmed to the idea that reservations are required at lauded venues. “People seek out some bars for a specific drink that they’ve seen online or maybe even a dish that the bar has,” says schmuck. co-owner Moe Aljaff. “So, I think they’re more willing to make a reservation like they do with restaurants.”

But as reservations in bars become more commonplace, venues often struggle to strike the right balance between reserved tables and walk-ins. When door policies become too rigid, it’s often at the expense of service, causing frustration among guests who expect more flexibility from a bar than a restaurant.

Balancing Reservations with Walk-ins

Before Sip & Guzzle opened in 2024, the initial plan was to forgo reservations altogether. The owners hoped that the bifurcated design — with a more casual bar upstairs and a more refined lounge downstairs — would create a natural waiting area for walk-in guests, depending on which part of the bar they planned to visit. But having a more ambitious food program also meant the kitchen needed to plan ahead; not knowing how many guests to expect on any given night would be problematic for the chef. “In the beginning, we held fewer tables back [for walk-ins] because we didn’t know what the demand was going to be,” says Justin Weitz, one of Sip & Guzzle’s founding partners. “That gave us that extra security, but we found very quickly that going so reservation-heavy was making it impossible to accommodate walk-ins. We don’t want to be a place that turns people away.”

Notoriety can make it difficult to find balance between accommodating out-of-town guests and being accessible to locals. “At first, we operated completely on a first-come, first-served basis,” says Valerie Carrasco, director of operations for Scotch Lodge in Portland, Ore. “We wanted to allow time to get a feel for the neighborhood and understand the flow of service. Once we got settled in, we found that offering some reservations would be helpful for guests looking to plan a bit further in advance for special occasions or guests visiting from out of town.”

“I think putting time constraints on reservations adds to the anxiety of going out for people. It can really work against you [as a bar] if you’re not properly training people on how to explain your policies.”

Rather than reserving the entire bar, schmuck. allocates a small tranche of early and late reservations during the week to accommodate guests that might not be willing to make the trip without a firm commitment. “There are a lot of people who come in from Long Island or Staten Island,” Aljaff says. “If they make that trip and then they’re told it’s impossible to get in, that’s a real bummer.” New Yorkers may be less inclined to traverse the boroughs late at night without assurances that a table will be available. So, giving the option to make a reservation after 10 p.m. incentivizes them to book in advance while also ensuring the bar stays full.

Leveraging Reservation Platforms For Efficiency

Like most restaurants these days, many top bars deploy reservation platforms like Resy and OpenTable which have built-in features to help them run more efficiently and maximize revenue per seat. “When we do availability planning on the back end, OpenTable notifies us that on average our turn times are seven minutes shorter than what we had preset,” says Alex Jump, co-owner of the Peach Crease Club in Denver. “Then we can decide whether or not to adjust based on that data. Initially, I think we had slightly longer turn times planned for two-tops, and we just shortened it a little bit.”

These platforms also help streamline customer relations management. “Reservations are great as a communication tool. The software gives us options to Google people or connect to their LinkedIn profile page,” says Jump. “It’ll tell us what they frequently drink or order at other places. It’ll also tell you if somebody left a bad review, so you can try to leave a better impression next time.”

When it better serves guests, Aljaff isn’t afraid to make last minute adjustments to the template on the backend. “During the last heat wave, we decided to open up more tables for reservations so people wouldn’t have to deal with the lines outdoors,” he says. “When we posted about it on our socials, the tables got booked up within an hour or so.”

The Rise of the 90-Minute Turn

Offering reservations often forces bars to adopt stricter policies around how much time is allotted for each party. Kumiko in Chicago notifies guests of the 90-minute time limit on their table when they make a reservation. But since food is so integral to the experience, predicting how much each party will eat or drink can be difficult. “When we call our reservations beforehand to confirm, we prompt them for more information about their evening — whether they plan to have dinner or drinks or if they have dinner reservations somewhere else,” says owner Julia Momosé. “Then we can account for that in terms of how much time we allot for their table.”

At The Wig Shop in Boston, guests are reminded of the 90-minute time limit at the door when they arrive. Since there is no seated bar inside for guests to wait, problems turning tables can lead to logjams of frustrated guests by the entrance. “Trying to explain to someone from Boston that they can’t sit at the bar is one of the biggest challenges,” says beverage director Oscar Simoza.

“At the end of the day, people don’t want to be rushed through their experience and we try very hard to make Kumiko the kind of place that you don’t want to leave.”

The constant pressure to turn tables without making guests feel rushed can be daunting. “If we have to, we’ll touch base with guests and let them know that the table is promised to another party, so if they want to order more food or drinks they have ample time,” says Momosé. “Sometimes that’s the nudge they need. Sometimes people push back. Sometimes they’re downright nasty.”

Since being included among the World’s 50 Best Bars in North America, Kumiko is attracting more international guests. Momosé says it can be harder to enforce time limits when guests come from countries where being asked to relinquish the table in a timely manner isn’t part of their culture. “From what I understand, reservations are less common for bars in Europe and Asia, so there can be more misunderstanding around reservations with international guests,” she says.

Aljaff finds that New Yorkers tend to be more accepting of the need to return the table, compared to his experience in Barcelona, where he opened Two Schmucks in 2017. (He left the bar in 2022.) “If you try to flip a table in Spain, you’ll be cursed out by the Spanish,” he says. “They’ll sit and have a vermouth for like 2 hours, and if you try anything you’ll have an earful. Here, it seems that people are much more empathetic and understanding that if the bar is really busy and they’re finished, they can just pay up and give the table to someone else.”

Has Reservation Culture Gone Too Far?

While the need to turn tables is more urgent than ever amid rising costs and declining alcohol consumption, some bar owners believe that reservation culture has gotten out hand, and that normalizing ruthless time limits compromises the guest experience.

“None of our bars have time limits,” says Meaghan Dorman, bar director and partner at Dear Irving and Raines Law Room in NYC. “I think putting time constraints on reservations adds to the anxiety of going out for people. It can really work against you [as a bar] if you’re not properly training people on how to explain your policies.” The increasing need to make a reservation at top bars, Dorman says, also makes impromptu visits less likely. “I think popping in for a drink shouldn’t lose that magic of spontaneity.”

Accolades like inclusion on the World’s 50 Best list can put more pressure on top bars to offer reservations or empower them to implement firmer policies that compromise hospitality. As cocktail enthusiasts rely more on these best-of lists to dictate where to imbibe, previously casual spots can be swarmed with clout chasers. The fame that comes along with being a buzzy new bar can force businesses to rethink their seating strategies, often leaving them unprepared for the realities of being a global destination with the constant pressure of catering to expectant crowds.

Michael Aredes, who has bartended at New York City hotspots like Superbueno and Nightmoves, sees an increasing number of top bars treating guests impersonally. “There are a few very famous bars that have time limits on their seats and they remind guests every 15 minutes that they have to leave at a certain time,” he says. “And it comes across like they see you as just a number. There’s a very fine line between hospitality and hostility.”

For bars that rely heavily on reservations, managing guest expectations is a constant struggle. And allowing guests open-ended visits isn’t viable for every business, especially bars that are trying to offer a more elevated experience. “We talk a lot about these issues during pre-shift meetings,” says Momosé. “At the end of the day, people don’t want to be rushed through their experience and we try very hard to make Kumiko the kind of place that you don’t want to leave.”

title: We Asked 9 Chefs: What’s Your Go-to Fast Food Order?
summary:
There’s nothing like digging into the bottom of a greasy bag to pull out a handful of fries at the end of a long day — even chefs who spend hours delicately placing herbs on a plate with tweezers can admit it. Whether it’s chicken nuggets with an array of dipping sauces, tacos topped with orange shredded cheese, or a specialty that you can only find at a local chain, these indulgent meals are delicious in a pinch. Sometimes, what’s in the bag doesn’t even matter. The nostalgia factor alone is enough to feed a craving.

content:
There’s nothing like digging into the bottom of a greasy bag to pull out a handful of fries at the end of a long day — even chefs who spend hours delicately placing herbs on a plate with tweezers can admit it.

Whether it’s chicken nuggets with an array of dipping sauces, tacos topped with orange shredded cheese, or a specialty that you can only find at a local chain, these indulgent meals are delicious in a pinch. Sometimes, what’s in the bag doesn’t even matter. The nostalgia factor alone is enough to feed a craving.

So we asked chefs with the most discerning palates for their go-to fast food orders. From national chains that they think actually do it right to throwback picks that have been powering them through shifts since their line cook days, here’s what nine chefs order when they pull up to the drive-thru.

The best go-to fast food orders, according to chefs:

  • White Castle Sliders
  • Wendy’s No. 6 Combo
  • Taco Bell bean burrito and Baja Blast
  • El Mago de las Fritas Cuban Fritas
  • Shake Shack Double ShackBurger
  • Taco Bell Mexican Pizza Combo
  • Fatso’s Last Stand Char Dog and a quarter pound of fried shrimp
  • Five Guys Burger
  • Wendy’s Chicken Nuggets
  • Gotham Burger Social Club Smash Burger

“My go-to is White Castle. Those sliders were so unique and distinctive to me as a kid, and those flavors still resonate today — there’s something about the onions steaming right into the beef that makes them so good. It’s actually the same technique we use with our Gotham Smash at Gotham Burger Social Club. That’s what inspired our motto: Nothing tastes better than memories.” —Mike Puma, owner, Gotham Burger Social Club, New York City

“Early in cooking, the No. 6 at Wendy’s was always my go-to meal after a long shift. The spicy chicken actually had a bit of a kick and the edges were super crispy. Fries, a diet Coke, and a chocolate frosty filled out the meal. Tasty, filling, and affordable.” —Chris McLaurin, chef, Lutra Cafe & Bakery, Durham, N.C.

“My go-to fast food order will always be Taco Bell: a bean burrito with potatoes, rice, and pico de gallo, washed down with a crisp Baja Blast. When I first started working in hospitality, the last thing I wanted to do after a long shift was go home and cook for myself. Taco Bell is consistent, quick, cheap, and filling. Nothing glamorous, but after a long day taking care of everyone else, it was exactly what I needed: comfort.” —Rayven Mendoza, director of culinary operations, Isla & Co. and Ms. Alice, NYC

“My favorite fast-food order is two Cuban fritas with Swiss cheese and everything on them, with a batido de mamey to wash it all down. It’s simple, nostalgic, and one of those meals I never get tired of. My favorite frita spot in Miami is El Mago de las Fritas. I remember going there as a kid with my dad and watching ‘El Mago’ working behind the counter. The combination of the seasoned meat and sauce is what makes the frita special. You get the soft Cuban bread against the crunch of the papitas, the richness of the meat and melted Swiss, and all those textures and flavors coming together in every bite.” —Gustavo Montes, executive chef, Yamashiro, Miami

“My go-to fast food order has got to be a Double ShackBurger. The original Shake Shack in Madison Square Park is the way to go, you really can’t beat it. Grab a couple of friends, have one person brave the line, and get a few orders of the crinkle-cut fries. When conceptualizing the menu at Sadie’s, I wanted to make sure our burger gave that same feeling: approachable, reliable, and always a crowd-pleaser.” —Jeffrey Marks, executive chef, Sadie’s, NYC

“Taco Bell, Mexican Pizza combo. I know the Mexican pizza isn’t what it used to be, but it’s still good. I order the Mexican pizza and two tacos supreme. Or for a local pick, if it’s Fatso’s, I order a char dog with everything. No fries, instead I go with a quarter pound of fried shrimp.” —John Manion, chef, El Che Steakhouse & Bar and Brasero, Chicago

“Honestly, I hate to admit this publicly, but when I do indulge in a burger once in a blue moon, I’m a Five Guys or Shake Shack guy. They both just do it right, it’s that simple. Good-quality ingredients, straightforward cooking techniques, and a burger that’s tasty, satisfying, and fast. You really don’t need much more than that. At Five Guys, I keep it simple. A single burger with American cheese and onions, plus some fries to share. At Shake Shack, I’ll go with a classic ShackBurger and, again, split the fries. Maybe it’s a boring order, but I think there’s something to be said for a fast-food chain that knows exactly what it does well and doesn’t overcomplicate it. When the ingredients are good and the execution is right, you don’t need to dress it up.” —Franklin Becker, head chef and owner, Point Seven, NYC

“It might sound silly, but I never liked fast food burgers or sandwiches as a kid. I’d always get a chicken nugget meal with Dr. Pepper, fries, and barbecue sauce. I’m definitely less selective now when it comes to late night munchies, but I’m still choosing chicken nuggets, preferably Wendy’s nugs.” —Joey Rosato, lead line cook, Kinda Nice, Brooklyn

“I love Gotham Burger Social Club in NYC. The Gotham Smash is a nostalgic smash burger with grilled onions, melted american cheese, housemade pickles, jalapeños, club sauce, ketchup, and mustard. I order it without jalapeños just because I’m getting old and if I don’t carry some Tums it’s probably not the best choice. It’s like going to the big arches but a thousand times better and not feeling guilty at all.” —Fabian Von Hauske, consulting chef, Ray’s, NYC

title: All of the Cocktails Named After U.S. States, Mapped
summary:
Whether it be for a big sporting event or community get together, sometimes an occasion calls for a cocktail with a little state pride. While each U.S. state has its most popular drink and perhaps a cocktail that matches the region’s vibes, many states also boast a namesake quaff. From the bullfrog-populous Connecticut to Kentucky’s bourbon country to the apple orchards of Washington State, some of these cocktails pull inspiration from the flora, fauna, and history of the land.

The article All of the Cocktails Named After U.S. States, Mapped appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Whether it be for a big sporting event or community get together, sometimes an occasion calls for a cocktail with a little state pride. While each U.S. state has its most popular drink and perhaps a cocktail that matches the region’s vibes, many states also boast a namesake quaff.

From the bullfrog-populous Connecticut to Kentucky’s bourbon country to the apple orchards of Washington State, some of these cocktails pull inspiration from the flora, fauna, and history of the land. On the other hand, a few of these drinks happen to share a name by pure coincidence — the New York Sour, for example, was actually created in Chicago, and is far from the most iconic cocktail of the Empire State.

We compiled all of the cocktails named after U.S. states, from classics like the Alaska to lesser-known libations like the Colorado Bulldog, and charted them in the map below. So grab your map and your mixing glass and get ready to sip your way across these U.S. states.

Alabama

While the Yellowhammer might be Alabama’s unofficial cocktail, its rhyming cousin — the Alabama Slammer — actually bears the state’s name. The cocktail mixes orange juice, sloe gin, whiskey, and amaretto into a highball glass, dressed up with a Maraschino cherry and an orange wheel. As the name suggests, this cocktail is a strong one, but fruit juice brings a sweet, acidic lift and balances out the three types of booze in this drink.

Alaska

The Alaska first appeared in bartender Jacques Straub’s seminal book “Straub’s Manual of Mixed Drinks,” published in 1913. Cocktail historians debate the origin of the drink’s name, though most agree it was a nod to the state’s 1896 Gold Rush: The Alaska has a bright, almost incandescently yellow hue. The aromatic cocktail is a combination of gin, yellow Chartreuse, and orange bitters, garnished with an orange twist.

Arizona

Bartender Mike O’Leary invented the Arizona Statehood in 1910 to honor a major step Congress took in making Arizona an official state. Arizona gained statehood two years later. The original recipe called for whiskey, fortified wine Dubonnet, Angostura bitters, gum syrup, and ginger ale. Modern tweaks contemporized the cocktail, which is now a combination of whiskey, bitters, Lillet Rouge, ginger syrup, and tonic water.

California

Bartender Alex Day invented the Alta California at New York City’s legendary cocktail bar Death & Co. in 2009. The cocktail brings together tequila, blanc vermouth, yellow Chartreuse, and cinnamon syrup in a coupe glass.

Colorado

The Colorado Bulldog is essentially a White Russian punched up with a squirt of Coca-Cola. The dive bar classic grew in popularity upon the advent of the soda gun machine. How the drink was invented and christened with its unconventional name is known, but many believe it first popped up at college bars near Colorado State University.

Connecticut

The Connecticut Bullfrog pays homage to the Constitution State’s high population of amphibians. The cocktail mixes gin, rum, lemon juice, and maple syrup — an even, but boozy, balance of herbaceous, sweet, and acidic flavors.

Hawaii

While many tropical cocktails might be associated with this state, only the Blue Hawaii shares its name. Pulling inspiration from the beachy cocktail trope — rum, blue Curaçao, pineapple juice, and lime juice are garnished with a pineapple wedge and cocktail umbrella — this drink is where tropical fruit meets booze. It also includes vodka, simple syrup, and lemon juice.

Kentucky

The Kentucky Mule is exactly what it sounds like: A Moscow Mule with bourbon in exchange for vodka. The caramel-forward flavor profile of the Kentucky-native brown spirit gives a warm, softer edge to the ginger beer and lime’s mouth-puckering bite.

The Kentucky Buck is the Kentucky Mule’s fruitier cousin. It brings together muddled strawberries, simple syrup, bourbon, lemon juice, ginger beer, and Angostura bitters. Served in a highball glass, this sipper is as sweet as it is sessionable.

The Kentucky Colonel made its debut in the cocktail canon in 1913 in “Straub’s Manual of Mixed Drinks,” but new iterations have adapted the cocktail to modern palates and techniques. The cocktail is a simple build: Four parts bourbon to one part Bénédictine meet in a rocks glass with a lemon twist.

The Kentucky River is an Old Fashioned riff that might irritate the classic whiskey cocktail’s staunch traditionalists, mixing bourbon with crème de cacao and peach bitters, garnished with a lemon twist. Built exactly like its predecessor, the Kentucky River’s off-kelter ingredients bring new complexities to the tried-and-true classic.

Louisiana

With its French name and ingredients, À La Louisiane is a tribute to New Orleans’ roots. A mixture of absinthe, Bénédictine, Peychaud’s bitters, sweet vermouth, and rye, this booze-forward cocktail melds herbaceous, sweet, and earthy flavors into a Nick & Nora.

Maine

The Remember the Maine is the lovechild of two rye whiskey classics: the Manhattan and the Sazerac. As outlined in “The Gentleman’s Companion,” a 1939 cocktail recipe and history book by Charles H. Baker, Jr., the rink is a nod to a sunken U.S. battleship. The Remember the Maine begins with rinsing a glass with absinthe before adding in rye, sweet vermouth, and cherry liqueur.

Mississippi

The Mississippi Bourbon Punch is a celebration of all-things south of the Mason-Dixon line. Muscadine wine — made from grapes abundant in Alabama and Mississippi — and bourbon make up the drink’s base. Grenadine along with orange, cranberry, and lime juice bring sweet, fruity edges to the quaff. The drink is topped with lemon-lime soda and club soda for a piquant effervescence.

Missouri

English bartender Joe Gilmore crafted the Missouri Mule in tribute to U.S. President Harry Truman in 1947. Gilmore worked at the famed Savoy Hotel American Bar in London, where Truman would frequent while visiting the British capital. Truman, a Missouri native, often opted for bourbon, making it the base spirit in this Mule. Its other ingredients include apple brandy, Campari, and Cointreau.

New York

While there’s a suite of libations named after Manhattan and the city’s many neighborhoods, the entire state gets a namesake cocktail, too. The New York Sour is a riff on the Whiskey Sour, sporting the classic combination of whiskey, lemon juice, simple syrup, and egg whites, but topped with a float of red wine. Even though this drink bears the New York name, it was widely believed to be invented in Chicago.

Oklahoma

The Oklahoma Club Special is a go-to choice in its home state. As the story goes, bartenders at a country club invented the drink to quench the thirsts of heat-exhausted golfers. Also abbreviated to the Club Special, the cocktail mixes vodka, limeade, lemon-lime soda, and club soda.

Rhode Island

The Rhode Island Red is a juicy and slightly boozy drink perfect for sipping along the sea-salty coast of its namesake state. It combines blanco tequila, Chambord raspberry liqueur, orange bitters, lemon juice, agave nectar, and ginger beer. Garnished with both a lemon and lime twist, the Rhode Island Red is refreshing, crisp, and fruity.

South Dakota

If a Beertini — beer with some olive brine — met with a Bloody Mary, it’d be the South Dakota Martini. In this drink, Bloody Mary mix and olive brine spice up a light lager, and the ensemble is speared with a pickle or dotted with an olive.

Tennessee

Similar to the Kentucky’s bourbon-spiked riff, the Moscow Mule gets a Volunteer State spin in the Tennessee Mule. With Tennessee whiskey, ginger beer, and lime juice, this drink adds a silky texture and warm flavors to the otherwise bright, acidic classic.

Texas

Everyone knows the Long Island Iced Tea as the ultimate kitchen-sink cocktail, but the Texas Tea also brings a host of different spirits together into a single glass. Similar to its northern counterpart, the concoction combines vodka, gin, rum, tequila, and triple sec with lemon juice, simple syrup, and cola, but the Lone Star State version adds a half ounce of bourbon for a slightly more southern twist.

Utah

Bartender Erick Castro invented the Johnny Utah — named after Keanu Reeves’ character in the blockbuster “Point Break” — in San Diego, Calif. The effervescent cocktail is a combination of tequila, celery seed syrup, lime juice, simple syrup, absinthe, and seltzer.

Vermont

One of the earliest accounts of the Old Vermont was in David Embury’s “The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks,” published in 1949, comparing it to another, similar cocktail. The Old Vermont combines London Dry gin, orange and lemon juice, and Angostura bitters with maple syrup, the state’s signature sweetener,.

Virginia

Named after the Rolling Stones’ crooning, harmonica-blowing hit track, the Sweet Virginia is a mix-match of saccharine spirits. Bourbon, cherry liqueur, curaçao, and sweet vermouth are at its base, with pineapple juice and bitters bringing a piquant, acidic punch.

Washington

The Washington Apple Cocktail allegedly emerged in the 1980s after a swarm of insects ravaged through the state’s apple orchards. Christof Guycoogan repurposed a bunch of rotting apples into schnapps and mixed them with Canadian whisky, and the result was the Washington Apple Cocktail, which includes cranberry juice in addition to the schnapps and whisky.

Wisconsin

The Wisconsin Old Fashioned is one of the most popular cocktails in the Midwest. What makes this version distinctive from the classic whiskey cocktail is the use of Korbel, a light-bodied domestic brandy, as its base spirit. The drink also includes a sugar cube muddled with Angostura bitters, lemon lime soda, and two Maraschino cherries.

title: AriZona Iced Tea’s New Artist Residency Is the Latest Chapter in Its Unconventional Brand Story
summary:
Any marketing executive will tell you that they care about their brand’s aesthetics, but it’s rare to find a corporation where the design language is as distinctive, long-lasting, and personal as AriZona Iced Tea — a commitment that has recently taken an unexpected turn. AriZona Iced Tea entered the market in 1992 with cans featuring an eye-catching palette of teal and green and motifs inspired by the American Southwest, all of which still feature prominently everywhere from individual bottles and cans to the company’s website and sprawling merchandise store.

The article AriZona Iced Tea’s New Artist Residency Is the Latest Chapter in Its Unconventional Brand Story appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Any marketing executive will tell you that they care about their brand’s aesthetics, but it’s rare to find a corporation where the design language is as distinctive, long-lasting, and personal as AriZona Iced Tea — a commitment that has recently taken an unexpected turn.

AriZona Iced Tea entered the market in 1992 with cans featuring an eye-catching palette of teal and green and motifs inspired by the American Southwest, all of which still feature prominently everywhere from individual bottles and cans to the company’s website and sprawling merchandise store. Take away all the words and it’s still obvious which brand it is — the visual language is that distinctive. Even the company’s logo is essentially unchanged since 1992.

For consumers of the time, the maximalist Southwest style set the new products apart from the more formulaic packaging of competitors like Snapple and Nestea. It was all the more compelling because it built on the founders’ own stylistic preferences and vision, not those of focus groups and consultants.

“We designed it in-house with a scratch pad and pencils and markers, and came up with what we thought was a cool look,” co-founder Don Vultaggio told The Washington Post at the time, and his wife, Ilene, was the artist who inspired the cherry blossom motif on the packaging for the company’s green tea. Before getting into the beverage business, the couple had also incorporated Southwest themes in the interior design of their own home.

A New Chapter in Company Branding

“Art and design have always been an important part of AriZona’s visual identity,” says Spencer Vultaggio, AriZona’s present-day chief marketing officer (Don and Ilene’s son), explaining the company’s latest ventures in captivating aesthetics, which have recently focused on in-person experiences.

In 2024, a new facility called AriZonaLand opened its doors in Keasbey, N.J. as both a bottling plant and visitor center with over-the-top decor including indoor artificial trees, a floor covered in the teal-and-cherry-blossom pattern from the green tea cans, and all manner of pink and yellow accents.

“Having access to a genuine community of people whose common goal is to create together, support, and uplift each other is hard to come by these days.”

Over the last year-plus, AriZona has hosted an artist residency program at its headquarters in Woodbury, N.Y., with up to four artists in each six-week-long session. The first cohort began its residency in July 2025, and the program just wrapped up its third group this August, with four participants making art and building connections. The artists receive a stipend, living space, materials, and access to AriZona’s rooftop studio and shop.

In keeping with the founders’ deeply personal approach to building the brand all those years ago, AriZona’s residency is truly immersive and hands-on, with participants working closely with each other and company creatives, with ideas allowed to flow freely and take unexpected turns.

“Having access to a genuine community of people whose common goal is to create together, support, and uplift each other is hard to come by these days,” Vultaggio says. “We hope this program fosters meaningful connections and helps alleviate some of the pressures of everyday life.”

There’s also a business angle: like AriZona’s famous commitment to keeping its cans of iced tea priced at 99 cents, the residency is an attention-grabbing way to set the company apart, using quirkiness as a competitive advantage and marketing tactic.

“I often take breaks to collaborate with the other artists, discuss our concepts, and offer feedback on each other’s work. It’s been fascinating to see how each person has mastered their own medium.”

“The program also reflects AriZona’s commitment to doing things differently,” Vultaggio says. “Inviting artists to work on site, giving them the time, space, resources, and creative freedom to make new work is something uncommon within the corporate world.”

A Day in the Life of an Artist in Residence

For the participants, the residency offers inspiration and connection. “I spend the day developing projects, experimenting with new ideas, and making the most of the full workday,” says Eleanor Dexter, a member of the most recent group, who has used the time to develop a collection of paintings and silkscreen projects. “I often take breaks to collaborate with the other artists, discuss our concepts, and offer feedback on each other’s work. It’s been fascinating to see how each person has mastered their own medium.”

 

There’s also the physical workspace, a spacious workshop known as The Lookout, which AriZona’s own creative team also uses and is fully outfitted with tools and technology from computer workstations to a woodshop. Another member of the recent cohort, a textile, wood, and metal artist named Lucas Carlo Monasterio, has been working with one of AriZona’s employees on a project that involves laser-cutting leather, in addition to a sculpture involving wood and steel. “My dream is to work on a larger scale of community projects,” he says. “Working in the shop during this residency was a great first step.”

Building Careers, Building a Brand

As the artists work on their own projects and take the next steps in their own careers, they often draw inspiration from their surroundings. AriZona showcases the work in an exhibition at the end of each session and highlights its work on social media; the company also invites artists to contribute a piece to its permanent collection. The results are often a mix of both deeply personal expressions and nods to the corporate context, like large-scale reinterpretations of iced-tea cans or riffs on Ilene’s cherry-blossom pattern.

One recent participant, Anna Fleury, made a stained-glass window with a Southwest-inspired design featuring a cactus and cow skull, which is now the focal point of a door in the workspace. Fleury says she hadn’t even intended to work on stained glass before the residency — but once she was on-site and saw the tools and materials available, she felt inspired: “That led to a series of projects, including a cherry blossom stained glass panel, stained glass juice boxes with hand-painted enamel designs, stained glass hot air balloons, and a glass landscape inspired by the rooftop Lookout studio.”
Fleury’s work highlights the symbiosis at play in AriZona artist residency: it’s an ongoing dialogue between groups of artists and the brand itself, a way for everyone involved to play, create, and add to their legacy.

With all that work and all those conversations and collaborations, it’s natural that everyone needs a refreshment now and then — and, yes, AriZona does provide unlimited access to iced tea and other company products. (“I tried to work my way through as many AriZona flavors as I could during the residency!” says Fleury.) But unlike so many other corporate partnerships, those particular ice-cold beverages aren’t consumed for smiling photo-ops and overt endorsements; they’re savored as the starting point for something bigger for both the artists and the company.

content:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have an update on a record breaking beer heist, a look at the biggest cocktail in sports during its peak season, and the announcement of Four Roses’ annual Small Batch release.

News to know:

  • Beer heist escalates: Last week, a truck carrying an estimated 40,000 pounds — the equivalent of over 50,000 cans — of Pabst Blue Ribbon beer was stolen in Montclair, Calif. According to reports, the scale of the robbery might make it the biggest beer heist in modern history. On Wednesday, Pabst CEO Greig DeBow made a statement that the company is offering up to $20,000 for information.
  • Honey Deuce-mania reaches a fever pitch: The US Open is in full swing in New York City, and that means our feeds are clogged with photos of bright pink, melon ball-adorned Honey Deuces. Naturally, celebs are in on the action, with a notable activation between Grey Goose — the vodka brand behind the iconic drink — and NBA champion Josh Hart. Though known for his love of fine wine, the beloved Knicks player teamed up with the brand in a social media video showcasing him as the “ultimate baller” meticulously carving out melon balls for the cocktail’s labor intensive garnish. With the tournament slinging 738,459 Honey Deuces in 2025 — topping the previous year by a 32 percent increase — it’s clear this summer trend is only continuing to rise.

Product releases to watch:

  • Four Roses announces release of annual Small Batch series: The 19th edition of the Four Roses Limited Edition Small Batch will launch on October 10, with a barrel-strength blend that features bourbons aged up to 23 years. The blend brings together several hand-selected batches, showcasing three of the distillery’s 10 distinct recipes at different ages, including the 14-year-old OBSK, 14-year-old OESK, 15-year-old OESV, and 23-year-old OESK. The whiskey is non-chill filtered and bottled at 109.2 proof. A coveted, limited-edition release, only about 16,800 bottles will be available at select retailers nationwide for a suggested retail price of $249.
  • Liquid Death founder launches canned sparkling wine with Sazerac: In a massive aesthetic shift, Mike Cessario, founder of punk rock canned water company Liquid Death, is partnering with Sazerac to launch a new canned sparkling wine called Mr. Fancy. The can of “American Bubbly” comes in at 5.5 percent ABV and will come in both Brut and Rosé varieties. A 6-pack will be available for a suggested retail price of $14.99.
  • A bourbon for birthdays: On Wednesday, Old Forester announced the release of its annual limited edition Birthday Bourbon, which commemorates the September 2 birthday of founder George Garvin Brown, who opened the distillery in 1870. The 2026 expression was bottled at 11 years old at 97 proof and will be available in limited qualities for a suggested retail price of $200. This year the brand also collaborated with Alpha Industries to design a specialty jacket to go along with the release, which will be available online on September 10 for $250.
  • Whiskey with seasoning: On Thursday, Woodford Reserve announced the debut of its 2026 Master’s Collection. The Super Seasoned Oak bottling, crafted under master distiller Elizabeth McCall, marks the 22nd release under the distillery’s experimental series, introducing an unconventional method for seasoning the barrels. Traditional bourbon barrels rely on white oak seasoned in the open air for up to one year, the Super Seasoned Oak expression uses staves exposed to the elements for five to seven years, adding a rich depth of flavor. The whiskey is bottled at 100.4 proof and will be available for a suggested retail price of $179.99 for a 700-milliliter bottle.

title: 12 Honey Deuce Riffs to Try at NYC Bars This US Open Season
summary:
To some, peak melon season means biting into sweet and juicy slices of honeydew on the beach. To tennis fans, the ripe summer fruit signals that it’s time to knock back a Honey Deuce. Star tennis players of the US Open come and go, but the one darling of the tournament that makes an appearance year after year is the iconic pink cocktail made with Grey Goose Vodka, lemonade, and raspberry liqueur.

The article 12 Honey Deuce Riffs to Try at NYC Bars This US Open Season appeared first on VinePair.
content:
To some, peak melon season means biting into sweet and juicy slices of honeydew on the beach. To tennis fans, the ripe summer fruit signals that it’s time to knock back a Honey Deuce. Star tennis players of the US Open come and go, but the one darling of the tournament that makes an appearance year after year is the iconic pink cocktail made with Grey Goose Vodka, lemonade, and raspberry liqueur.

The Honey Deuce — with its signature garnish of three melon balls — has become so popular among US Open attendees and viewers worldwide that now, bars serve riffs on the drink in time with the annual tournament. Grey Goose even partners with some bars to serve the original Honey Deuce in its branded, Instagrammable cup off the courts.

There’s no better place to enjoy a Honey Deuce or one of its spinoffs than in the US Open’s home base of New York City. Here are 12 Honey Deuce- and melon-inspired drinks to sip on this US Open season.

Clemente Bar: The Sour Love

Clemente Bar — the art-filled watering hole located above world-famous fine dining destination Eleven Madison Park — is honoring the tried-and-true vodka cocktail with the Sour Love. The cocktail brings together Grey Goose, tomato gin, aloe, and muskmelon liqueur with green tomato and watermelon juices. The concoction is then clarified with coconut milk. The result is less of a deuce than an all-out ace: The transparent cocktail, served in a rocks glass and garnished with a skewer of pickled watermelon and honeydew, gives a fresh, silky spin on the classic drink’s sweet, fruit-forward flavor profile.

Gem: The Honey Deuce Slushy

For a zero-proof Honey Deuce but with the same, familiar flavors, Nolita’s Gem proves that it isn’t just the booze that keeps fans coming back to the Honey Deuce — it’s the tangy, sweet-and-sour taste. Gem is currently offering a slushy, booze-free version of the drink. A mixture of honeydew, raspberry, and lemon juice come together in a piquant, tart, and refreshing frozen drink — served with a melon ball, of course.

Sake No Hana: The Love Set

 

Sake No Hana in Manhattan’s Lower East Side brings an elegant take on the courtside classic. The Love Set — a play on tennis terms — is a blend of sparkling wine and cassis with a muskmelon ball garnish. On the side comes an oyster studded with caviar, a briny complement to the currant-forward drink.

Muku: Morning Dew

At Muku, a kaiseki counter in Tribeca, beverage director Steve Kim adds a French and Japanese spin to the classic Honey Deuce. For the Morning Dew, he combines shochu, green Chartreuse, honeydew, citric acid, and ginger beer. The Morning Dew is built into a highball glass and adorned with a shiso flower.

Bar Blondeau: 40 Love Spritz

Another playful tennis pun, the 40 Love Spritz, served at the rooftop Bar Blondeau in Williamsburg, brings the flavors and appearance of a Honey Deuce into an entirely new frontier. The cocktail takes the original flavors of the Honey Deuce — vodka, Chambord raspberry liqueur, and lemon — but adds soda water to bring a fizzy, refreshing energy to the mix. The final product is a blush-pink spritz garnished with a pale-green cucumber, mimicking the colors of the original drink.

Bar Fiori: Deuces Wild

Bar Fiori, the accompanying cocktail lounge to Midtown’s Ai Fiori, is serving up a menu of sparkling cocktails in honor of the US Open called the Grand Slam Spritz. Paying homage to the vodka, lemonade, and raspberry classic is the Deuces Wild, all coming together in spritz form. The drink features melon liqueur, natural lemon flavor, lemongrass, and grapefruit juice.

Confidant: Lil’ Melon

Though it might not be an exact variation of the Honey Deuce, Confidant’s Lil’ Melon offers another great way to celebrant melon season. This cocktail ditches the honeydew for cantaloupe, imparting a rounder and more savory melon flavor. The bright-orange drink combines cantaloupe, cucumber gin, sherry, and lemon — a beautiful balance between sweet, savory, and funk. The garnish — skewered cantaloupe pieces — recall the classic honeydew balls that fans will find at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Forgione: Sake-Tini

Forgione beverage director Cara Patteson crafted the Sake-Tini with Haku vodka, sake, and a homemade honeydew and cucumber cordial. Served in a coupe and adorned with the signature skewer of three melon balls, this cocktail balances refreshing, floral qualities with boozy strength.

Beefbar: The Honey Deuce

Tribeca’s Beefbar collaborated with Grey Goose for beverage director Robert Giles to take a spin on the tournament classic. Beefbar’s Honey Deuce is a mixture of vodka, black raspberry liqueur, yuzu, and lemonade. The ensemble is garnished with the classic honeydew balls that are rolled in “electric dust,” a zingy salt mixture.

Queens Tavern: The English Garden Deuce

Queens Tavern in Hudson Yards also partnered with Grey Goose for a unique spin on the tennis lovers’ favorite. The English Garden Deuce brings vodka, dry vermouth, apple liqueur, honey, and lemonade together into the signature branded glass.

Elcielo: Elcielo New York Honey Deuce

Elcielo, a fine dining Columbian restaurant in Midtown, brings the flavors of the classic Honey Deuce with different ingredients and techniques. Honeydew soda, juice of the Southeast Asian-native kaffir lime, and raspberry-infused vodka come together for a light-bodied sipper.

The Tusk Bar: The Honey Deuce

Chic NoMad destination Tusk Bar — the cocktail-slinging appendage to the restaurant Brass — is featuring the Honey Deuce in an altogether new environment. If you don’t have the chance to sip it courtside, enjoy the same build in over a marble bar and beneath dim-lit chandeliers, served in a highball glass.
